name: Hee Bermiok
tagline: Limbu heritage, cardamom farms and forest walks west of Pelling
meta_description: Hee Bermiok (about 1,950 m): Limbu heritage at Martam, cardamom and orange farms, homestays and Kangchenjunga views in West Sikkim. Costs and how to reach.
summary: Hee Bermiok is a cluster of farming villages in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), climbing to about 1,950 m in the hills between Pelling and Dentam. It is known for cardamom and orange farms, homestays, forest walks and its Limbu heritage at nearby Martam, linked to the scholar Sirijunga. Stay 1–2 nights.
intro: Hee Bermiok is not one village but a spread of hamlets, fields and forest on a long slope west of Pelling, with Bermiok Bazar as its market. The upper villages sit at around 1,950 m and the lower fields drop well below that towards the river. Wikipedia describes it as a small town known for nature walks, hiking, mountain biking and the customs of the Limbu, Sherpa, Bhutia, Lepcha and Nepali communities who live here.

It is a farming place first. Black cardamom grows under shade trees on the slopes, and orange orchards fill the lower fields; in late autumn and winter the fruit ripens and the cardamom is dried in smoke houses. Families have opened homestays, and a few small hotels and a resort have come up, but it remains quiet, with the Kangchenjunga range visible from the upper villages on clear mornings. Evenings are early and quiet.

Hee Bermiok matters to the Limbu (Yakthung) community. Martam, near Bermiok Bazar, is linked with Te-ongsi Sirijunga, the 18th-century scholar who revived the Limbu script, and it has a Limbu community temple. The community gathers there each December around his birth anniversary. We send travellers here for two nights of village life, slow walks and good home food, often paired with Dentam, the Singshore Bridge and Uttarey further west, as a short circuit of West Sikkim's farming villages.

story.title: Sirijunga and the Limbu script
story.text: Te-ongsi Sirijunga was an 18th-century Limbu scholar who travelled through Limbuwan in eastern Nepal and into Sikkim teaching the Limbu script, language and the Mundhum, the Limbu body of oral scripture. Wikipedia's biography, which draws largely on Limbu tradition and is thinly referenced, says he was born in 1704 in today's Taplejung district of Nepal, entered Sikkim in 1734 and set up centres of learning, and was killed around 1741 at Kalej Khola in Hee-Martam, at a time of conflict between Limbu communities and the Sikkimese court and monasteries. The Wikipedia article on Hee Bermiok adds that the first Limbu community temple was built at Martam and inaugurated in 1996, and that every December, around his birth anniversary, the Limbu community gathers at the temple courtyard with prayers, priests' dances and Limbu and Nepali dances. Accounts of his life and death differ, so we tell it as the community remembers it. Ask your homestay hosts what Sirijunga means to them today; for many Limbu families in West Sikkim, the script he revived is a living part of their identity.
story.source: Wikipedia: Te-ongsi Sirijunga Xin Thebe; Hee Burmiok; Limbu script

little_known.fact: Wikipedia gives Sirijunga's death place as Kalej Khola in Hee-Martam, West Sikkim, around 1741–1742, and notes that the Nepal Philatelic Bureau has issued a postage stamp in his name.
The first Limbu community temple, according to Wikipedia's Hee Bermiok article, was built at Martam near Bermiok Bazar and inaugurated in 1996 by the then Chief Minister, Pawan Kumar Chamling.
Wikipedia lists Hee Bermiok in its category of mountain biking venues, alongside its better-known farming of black cardamom and oranges on the slopes.

highlights.title: Martam and the Limbu temple
highlights.text: Martam, near Bermiok Bazar, has the Limbu community temple that Wikipedia says was the first of its kind, inaugurated in 1996, and is linked with the scholar Sirijunga. Visit with your host or a local guide, ask before entering and dress modestly.

highlights.title: Cardamom and orange farms
highlights.text: Black cardamom grows under shade trees on the slopes, and orange orchards fill the lower fields. Cardamom is harvested from about August to October and dried in smoke houses; oranges ripen from November into January. Ask your host to show you round.

highlights.title: Dawn view of Kangchenjunga
highlights.text: From the upper villages, on clear mornings from October to March, the Kangchenjunga range shows across the forested ridges to the north. Step outside at first light with a cup of tea; cloud usually builds by mid-morning.

highlights.title: Forest and ridge walks
highlights.text: Paths climb from the villages through oak and rhododendron forest to the ridges above. A village guide can lead an easy 3–4 hour walk with views and good birding, best in the early morning in spring and autumn.

highlights.title: Homestay food
highlights.text: Meals are home-style and generous: rice, dal, seasonal greens, gundruk or kinema, pickles and often chicken or pork, with oranges in winter. Limbu kitchens are known for fermented foods; ask your host to explain what is on the plate.

how_to_reach.text: Local jeeps link Bermiok Bazar with Gyalshing and Jorethang, mostly in the morning, indicatively ₹100–250 a seat depending on the route. Your homestay can tell you current timings. A shared jeep from Siliguri to Jorethang, then a local jeep or small car, is the budget route.

From Pelling, roughly 1–1.5 hours, indicatively ₹2,000–3,000 one way. From Jorethang, about 2–2.5 hours through the hills. From Gangtok, about 130 km and 6–7 hours via Legship. Roads are narrow and winding; avoid driving after dark.

About 145–155 km and 6–7 hours via Melli and Jorethang, indicatively ₹6,000–8,000 by private car. NH10 closes after heavy rain; the alternative is via Darjeeling, adding 1–2 hours. Check current status before you travel.

costs: Village guide for a day walk
where_to_stay: Hee Bermiok has a number of family homestays spread across the villages, at indicatively ₹1,200–2,200 per person with meals, plus a few small hotels and a resort, which Wikipedia's article on the village mentions. Standards vary a great deal from one homestay to the next, so tell us what matters to you, such as an attached bathroom or a view, and we will match a family. For premium rooms, stay in Pelling at The Elgin Mount Pandim or Norbu Ghang Retreat and Spa and visit Hee Bermiok by day.
tips: Plan two nights: one is mostly arriving and leaving, the second gives you a full day of walks.
Visit in November to January for oranges, or August to October to see the cardamom harvest.
Ask before entering the Limbu temple at Martam, and do not photograph rituals without permission.
Carry cash; card and UPI payments are unreliable, and ATMs are in Gyalshing or Jorethang.
Pair Hee Bermiok with Dentam, the Singshore Bridge and Uttarey for a village circuit of 4–5 nights.

experiences.title: Martam and the story of Sirijunga
experiences.best_time: Year-round; December for the anniversary gathering
experiences.cost: ≈ ₹800–1,500 for a local guide; donation at the temple
experiences.summary: Visit Martam near Bermiok Bazar, linked with the 18th-century Limbu scholar Te-ongsi Sirijunga and home to a Limbu community temple, with a local guide who can explain the Limbu script, the Mundhum and what this place means to the community.
body: Martam is a small village near Bermiok Bazar with a large place in Limbu memory. Wikipedia's articles say Te-ongsi Sirijunga, who revived the Limbu script in the 18th century, was killed here around 1741, and that the first Limbu community temple was built at Martam and inaugurated in 1996.

Go with a local guide or your homestay host, ideally someone from the Limbu community, who can explain the script, the Mundhum oral scriptures recited by Limbu priests, and how Sirijunga is remembered. Ask before entering the temple and before taking photographs, dress modestly and leave a donation if it feels right.

If you are here in December, ask whether the community gathering for Sirijunga's anniversary is open to visitors; Wikipedia describes prayers, priests' dances and Limbu and Nepali dances in the temple courtyard. Dates and access are for the community to decide.

faqs.q: Who was Sirijunga?
faqs.a: Te-ongsi Sirijunga was an 18th-century Limbu scholar who taught and revived the Limbu script and collected Limbu literature in eastern Nepal and Sikkim. Wikipedia's biography, drawing largely on Limbu tradition, says he was born in 1704 in today's Taplejung district of Nepal and was killed at Hee-Martam in West Sikkim around 1741.

faqs.q: Can visitors enter the Limbu temple at Martam?
faqs.a: Visitors are generally welcome to see the temple from outside, and often inside, if they ask first and behave respectfully. Go with a local host or guide, dress modestly, remove shoes if asked and do not photograph people or rituals without permission. Access during ceremonies is at the community's discretion.

faqs.q: When is Sirijunga's anniversary celebrated at Martam?
faqs.a: Wikipedia's Hee Bermiok article says the Limbu community celebrates his birth anniversary each December at the temple courtyard, with prayers, priests' dances and Limbu and Nepali dances. Exact dates follow the community's own calendar, so ask your host or us close to your trip. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Cardamom groves and orange orchards walk
experiences.best_time: Aug–Oct for cardamom; Nov–Jan for oranges
experiences.cost: ≈ ₹800–1,500 for a guide; often free with your host
experiences.summary: Walk through the shade forests where Hee Bermiok's families grow black cardamom and through their orange orchards, and see how the crop is harvested and smoke-dried in the village, with your homestay host or a village guide.
body: Sikkim is one of the world's main growers of large or black cardamom, a tall plant that grows in shade under alder and other trees on moist slopes. Wikipedia notes Hee Bermiok as rich in cardamom and orange plantations, and both shape the village year and family incomes.

Your host or a village guide will take you into a cardamom grove, where the pods form in clusters at the base of the plant, and to the smoke houses, called bhatti, where the harvested pods are dried over a wood fire for several days. From November to January, walk through the orange orchards when the fruit ripens.
Ask about prices, plant diseases and how the crop has changed; farmers here are frank about both good and bad years. Buy cardamom or oranges directly from a family if you can.

faqs.q: When is the cardamom harvest in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: Large cardamom is usually harvested from about August to October, depending on altitude, with the pods then dried in smoke houses for several days. Visiting in September and October gives the best chance of seeing harvest and drying, although rain can still fall in September.

faqs.q: Can I buy cardamom and oranges in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Yes, in season you can often buy directly from farming families or in Bermiok Bazar. Cardamom keeps well and packs easily. Oranges are sold from November to January. Prices vary each year with the harvest and market; ask your host what is fair before you buy.

faqs.q: Is the farm walk suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes. It is a gentle walk on village paths, with plenty to look at and taste, and children usually enjoy the orchards. Some paths through the cardamom groves are steep and muddy, so wear shoes with grip. Watch for leeches in the wetter months of the harvest season.

experiences.title: Ridge and forest walk above the villages
experiences.summary: Climb from Hee Bermiok's upper villages through oak and rhododendron forest to the ridges above for valley views and, on clear mornings, the Kangchenjunga range, with a village guide and an eye out for birds.
body: Above the upper villages, paths climb through mixed forest of oak, chestnut and rhododendron to open ridges. With a village guide, an easy walk of three to four hours takes you up for views over the valleys towards Pelling and Dentam and, on clear mornings between October and March, north to the Kangchenjunga range.
Start early, when the air is clearest and the forest is full of birds: barbets, minivets, laughingthrushes and sunbirds are common. In March and April the rhododendrons flower along the higher paths.

The route is chosen on the day by your guide according to weather and the state of the paths. Carry water, a snack, a warm layer and a rain jacket, and wear shoes with good grip. Return for lunch at your homestay and a slow afternoon.

faqs.q: Can I see Kangchenjunga from Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Yes, on clear mornings, mostly from October to March, from the upper villages and the ridges above. The view is across forested ridges at a lower angle than from Pelling. Cloud usually builds by mid-morning, so be outside at first light. In the monsoon the range is rarely visible.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide for walks in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: For short walks around your homestay, no. For the forest and ridge paths, yes: trails branch often, cross private land and can be confusing in cloud. A village guide costs indicatively ₹800–1,500 for a few hours, knows the birds and plants, and keeps the money in the village.

faqs.q: What should I pack for walks in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Shoes with good grip, a warm layer, a rain jacket, a hat, sunscreen, water and snacks. Binoculars are worth bringing for birds. From June to September add leech socks or salt, and from December to February add gloves and thermals for the early starts.

experiences.title: Mountain biking on village roads and tracks
experiences.cost: Varies; bring or pre-arrange a bike
experiences.summary: Ride Hee Bermiok's quiet village roads and farm tracks on a mountain bike, with steep climbs, long descents and valley views; Wikipedia notes the area for mountain biking, but you will need to bring or pre-arrange a suitable bike.
body: Wikipedia's article on Hee Bermiok names mountain biking among its activities, and the terrain explains why: quiet village roads, farm tracks and steep gradients through forest and fields, with little traffic outside the morning jeep runs.

We have not found a reliable bike-hire service in the village, so plan this only if you bring your own bike or arrange one in advance through a specialist operator. Ride with a local who knows which tracks are open and safe, and wear a helmet.

Climbs are long and steep at nearly 2,000 m, so take it slowly on the first day. Avoid riding in rain, when roads become slippery and slides can block tracks, and give way to jeeps and walkers on narrow bends.

faqs.q: Can I hire a mountain bike in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: We have not found a reliable hire service in the village itself. If cycling is important to you, bring your own bike or arrange one through a specialist cycling operator in advance, and tell us so we can plan transport. Check current status before you travel, as local options may change.

faqs.q: How hard is mountain biking in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Demanding. Roads and tracks are steep, often rough and at around 1,500–2,000 m altitude, so even short climbs are hard work. Fit riders with mountain biking experience will enjoy it. Beginners should ride short sections with a support vehicle and walk the steepest climbs.

faqs.q: When is the best season for cycling in West Sikkim?
faqs.a: October to December, when roads are dry and skies clear, and March to April before the pre-monsoon rain. Avoid June to September, when rain, mud and landslides make roads dangerous, and expect cold mornings in December and January. Always carry rain gear in the hills.

faqs.q: Where is Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Hee Bermiok is a group of villages around Bermiok Bazar in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), in the hills between Pelling and Dentam. The upper villages sit at about 1,950 m. It is roughly 1–1.5 hours by car from Pelling, about 2–2.5 hours from Jorethang and about 6–7 hours from Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is Hee Bermiok known for?
faqs.a: Farm life and Limbu heritage. The slopes grow black cardamom and oranges, families run homestays, and paths lead into oak and rhododendron forest. Nearby Martam is linked with the Limbu scholar Sirijunga and has a Limbu community temple. Wikipedia also notes the area for mountain biking.

faqs.q: How many days should I spend in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Two nights is ideal: one full day for a forest walk in the morning and a farm or heritage visit in the afternoon. One night works as a stop between Pelling and Uttarey. For a longer village circuit, add Dentam, the Singshore Bridge and two or three nights in Uttarey.

faqs.q: Is Hee Bermiok good for families?
faqs.a: Yes, for families who enjoy simple village life. Children usually like the farms, orchards and animals, and the walks can be kept short. Homestays are basic and evenings quiet, with no shops or entertainment. Families who want hotel comforts should base in Pelling and visit by day.

faqs.q: Where can I stay in Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Mostly in family homestays across the villages, at indicatively ₹1,200–2,200 per person with meals, and there are a few small hotels and a resort. Standards vary, so ask us to match a homestay to your needs. Premium travellers usually stay in Pelling and visit by day.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: October to December for clear views, harvests and oranges, and March to May for flowers and birds. December and January bring cold nights but clear mornings and ripe oranges. June to September is wet, with leeches and landslides, though cardamom harvest begins in August.

faqs.q: How do I get to Hee Bermiok from Siliguri?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Jorethang, about 3–3.5 hours via Melli on NH10, then a local jeep or small car up to Hee Bermiok, about 2–2.5 hours more. A private car from NJP or Bagdogra takes about 6–7 hours. If NH10 is closed, the route goes via Darjeeling.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Hee Bermiok?
faqs.a: Indian citizens do not need a permit. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online through the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India. All tourists pay Sikkim's ₹50 entry fee, usually collected at check-in by hotels and homestays. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Limbu script?
faqs.a: The Limbu script, also called Sirijunga, is the writing system of the Limbu language, spoken in eastern Nepal and Sikkim. It was revived in the 18th century by Te-ongsi Sirijunga, who is linked with Martam near Hee Bermiok. In Sikkim, Limbu is one of the state's recognised languages, and you may see the script on signs and in schools.
